docs.title: LakeLogic MCP
docs.text:
Help AI assistants check and test data contracts locally.

Validate Open Lakehouse Contracts (OLC), find governance gaps, explain rules and generate sample data. Test-run contracts with LakeLogic Core using Polars or DuckDB, then inspect accepted rows, failed rows and the reasons they failed.

Works with MCP-compatible assistants — Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor and others. No LakeLogic account required.

OLC defines the contract. Core executes it. MCP gives your assistant access to those tools.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"Check orders.yaml, explain any findings, generate sample data and test it locally."

The assistant validates the contract, lints it, explains each finding, writes test data shaped by the contract, runs it, and reports which rows passed and why the others failed — real results from LakeLogic, not plausible-looking YAML.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text: Ask Tool Does it match the OLC model? validate_contract Does it pass the lint checks? lint_contract Why is this rule flagged? explain_rule How is this part of a contract written? contract_reference Give me the ODCS version export_odcs Make me test data for it generate_test_data What happens when it runs? run_contract

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
claude mcp add lakelogic -- uvx lakelogic-mcp

Start your assistant in the project that holds your contracts, then try the Walkthrough. Other clients: see Install. Before running contracts on real data, read Safety and privacy.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
Work on the server from a checkout, next to checkouts of open-lakehouse-contract and LakeLogic.

cd lakelogic-mcp
uv venv .venv
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python "mcp>=1.2" pytest -e ../open-lakehouse-contract -e ../lakelogic
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps -e .
.venv/bin/python -m pytest

On Windows use .venv\Scripts\python.exe.

docs.title: Use your checkout in Claude Code
docs.text:
From the project whose contracts you want checked:

claude mcp add lakelogic -- /path/to/lakelogic-mcp/.venv/bin/lakelogic-mcp

docs.title: The docs
docs.text:
This site is built with Material for MkDocs and published to GitHub Pages on every push to main.

pip install -r docs-requirements.txt
mkdocs serve      # http://127.0.0.1:8012

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
You need:

  • uv on your PATH. Every client starts the server with uvx, which downloads and runs it — no separate install.
  • Python 3.10 or later (uv can provide it).

The server works on one project folder: where your contracts are. Terminal clients start it in the folder you run them from; desktop apps do not, so give them --root.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
As a plugin:

/plugin marketplace add LakeLogic/lakelogic-mcp
/plugin install lakelogic-mcp@lakelogic-mcp

Or directly, from your project folder:

claude mcp add lakelogic -- uvx lakelogic-mcp

docs.title: Claude Desktop
docs.text:
Edit claude_desktop_config.json (Settings → Developer → Edit Config). It lives in %APPDATA%\Claude\ on Windows and ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/ on macOS.

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "lakelogic": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["lakelogic-mcp", "--root", "/path/to/your/contracts/project"]
    }
  }
}

Restart Claude Desktop after saving.

docs.title: Cursor
docs.text:
Add to Cursor, or edit .cursor/mcp.json in your project (or ~/.cursor/mcp.json for every project):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "lakelogic": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["lakelogic-mcp"]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
Edit .vscode/mcp.json in your project. VS Code's format differs: the top key is servers and each server names its type.

{
  "servers": {
    "lakelogic": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["lakelogic-mcp"]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Other MCP clients
docs.text:
Run uvx lakelogic-mcp as a stdio server, with --root <folder> if the client does not start it in your project. Check your client's documentation for where its MCP settings go.

The server is also listed in the official MCP Registry as io.github.LakeLogic/lakelogic-mcp.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Meaning --root <folder> The project folder the tools work in. Default: the folder the server starts in. LAKELOGIC_MCP_ROOT The same, as an environment variable.

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text: Ask your assistant "List the LakeLogic tools you have." It should name the seven tools on the Tools page. Then try the Walkthrough.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause and fix The client says it cannot start the server, or uvx is not found uv is not installed or not on the PATH the client sees. Install uv, then restart the client. On Windows a desktop app may need a sign-out to pick up a new PATH; or give the full path to uvx as the command. A tool says a file is outside the project, or cannot find your contract The server is working in a different folder. Set --root to the folder that holds your contracts (paths are relative to it). The assistant does not list the LakeLogic tools The server did not start, or the client was not restarted after the settings change. Restart the client and check its MCP log; in Claude Code, run claude mcp list. The first start is slow uvx downloads the package and its dependencies the first time. Later starts use the cache.

docs.title: Safety and privacy
docs.text: An assistant with tools can do things. This page says what these tools do, and where the limits are.

docs.title: The server
docs.text:
• Local. It talks to your MCP client over stdio. The server itself opens no network connection, needs no account and sends no telemetry. (Installing it with uvx downloads the package and its dependencies, like any install.)
  • Tool paths stay in your project. Every path given to a tool is resolved inside the folder the server was started in (or --root). A path that points outside it — including through .. — is refused. The _domain.yaml / _system.yaml that lint_contract takes into account are searched for only inside the project too.

docs.title: When a contract runs
docs.text:
run_contract hands the contract to LakeLogic Core, which does what the contract configures. Two things follow:

  • A contract can configure network calls. If it declares notifications (for example a Slack webhook) or run-log delivery to a service, Core may send them during the run. Run contracts you trust, or remove those blocks before a test run.
  • A contract can point at other files. Files the contract itself names — a reference dataset under links:, for example — are read by Core and are not limited to the project folder.

Nothing is written to the contract's target table either way.

docs.title: Files the tools write
docs.text:
These are the files the tools themselves save, all inside the project:

Tool Writes Where generate_test_data A synthetic data file test_data/ (or the output you give) run_contract No file of its own, unless write_outputs is set; then the good and quarantined rows runs/

This is separate from what Core does because the contract asks for it during run_contract (notifications, run-log delivery — see When a contract runs). write_outputs does not turn those on or off; a contract's own settings do.

Both tools are marked to the client as not read-only, so most clients ask before running them. The five other tools are marked read-only.

docs.title: What reaches your AI provider
docs.text:
Running locally does not keep results away from the assistant. Every tool result goes into the assistant's context, and so to whichever model provider your client uses. That includes:

  • run_contract's sample of quarantined rows (sample, default 10);
  • failure reasons and error messages, which can quote values from your data;
  • the contract itself whenever a tool reads or reports on it — field names, descriptions, rules.

Setting sample to 0 removes the row sample only; the rest is still returned. If a data file holds real personal or confidential data, test with generated data instead.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Seven tools. Five only read a contract and report; two act locally — one writes a test-data file, one runs a contract on a local file. Clients may call the read-only tools without asking each time (they are marked read-only to the client); the other two ask first in most clients.

Paths are files inside the project the server was started in. Every tool returns a JSON object. An expected problem — a missing file, a path outside the project, a bad argument — comes back as {"error": "..."}; a contract run that fails comes back as {"ran": false, "error": "..."}. Anything unexpected is reported by your MCP client as a tool error.

The server also tells the assistant how to use them together: after writing or changing a contract, validate, then lint, and fix what they report before showing it.

docs.title: validate_contract
docs.text:
Does it match the OLC model? Known keys, the right shapes, required fields.

Input Meaning path A contract file in the project contract_yaml Or the contract's text

Returns valid and, if not, each error's location and problem.

docs.title: lint_contract
docs.text:
Does it pass the lint checks? Governance gaps such as a merge with no key, unordered deduplication, untagged personal data, or a step no engine runs. Use after validate_contract passes.

Input Meaning path A contract file in the project contract_yaml Or the contract's text

Returns clean and findings, each with its rule code, severity and fix.

docs.title: explain_rule
docs.text:
Why does a lint rule exist? What it checks, why it matters, a failing contract and the fixed one.

Input Meaning code A lint rule code, e.g. KEY-002

docs.title: contract_reference
docs.text:
How is one part of a contract written? Returns the OLC reference page for that part.

Input Meaning topic One of: anatomy (every key), execution-order, ingestion, lifecycle, quality, security, compliance, transformation, external-logic, materialization, server, lineage, data-products, slo, notifications, extraction, conformance, cli, schema

docs.title: export_odcs
docs.text:
The contract as an Open Data Contract Standard document.

Input Meaning path A contract file in the project

docs.title: generate_test_data
docs.text:
Synthetic data shaped by the contract — the right types, accepted values and ranges — with a share of rows that deliberately break its quality rules, so a run shows quarantine working. Writes a file in the project.

Input Default Meaning path The contract file rows 100 How many rows invalid_ratio 0.1 Share of rows to make break a rule (requested; the response reports intended_invalid_rows, and run_contract shows how many actually fail) seed random For repeatable data output test_data/<contract>.csv Where to write it

docs.title: run_contract
docs.text:
What happens when it runs? Runs the contract on a local CSV or Parquet file with Polars or DuckDB: how many rows pass, how many are quarantined, and each quarantine reason with its count. Nothing is written to the contract's target. Core does what the contract configures, including any notifications — see Safety and privacy.

Input Default Meaning path The contract file source The data file (CSV or Parquet) in the project engine polars polars or duckdb sample 10 Maximum number of quarantined rows to return (accepted rows are never returned) write_outputs false Save the good and quarantined rows under runs/

A typical sequence: generate_test_data → run_contract on the file it wrote. See the Walkthrough for real output and how to read it.

docs.title: Walkthrough: your first contract
docs.text:
One small contract, start to finish: validate it, lint it, generate test data, run it, and read the result. The output below was captured from this exact example (lakelogic-mcp 0.1.3, seed=42). With another seed the IDs, and how the failures split between rules, will differ.

You can ask your assistant to do all of it in one go — "Check orders.yaml, generate 200 rows of test data with seed 42, run it and explain the result" — or call the tools one at a time as below.

docs.title: 1. The contract
docs.text:
Save this as orders.yaml in your project:

version: 1.0.0
dataset: orders
info:
  title: Orders
  owner: sales-data@example.com
  target_layer: silver
primary_key: [order_id]
model:
  fields:
    - {name: order_id, type: string, required: true}
    - {name: customer_id, type: string, required: true}
    - {name: status, type: string, required: true}
    - {name: amount, type: double, required: true}
quality:
  row_rules:
    - accepted_values: {field: status, values: [placed, shipped, delivered, cancelled]}
    - range: {field: amount, min: 0, max: 10000}

docs.title: 2. Validate — does it match the OLC model?
docs.text:
validate_contract(path="orders.yaml")

{ "contract": "orders.yaml", "valid": true, "errors": [] }

docs.title: 3. Lint — does it pass the lint checks?
docs.text:
lint_contract(path="orders.yaml")

{
  "contract": "orders.yaml",
  "clean": true,
  "findings": [
    {
      "rule": "VOL-001",
      "severity": "info",
      "message": "silver table has no freshness or volume SLO (contract or domain) — blind to stalled feeds / missing data.",
      "fix": "Add contract `service_levels.freshness`/`row_count`, or an `slo.*` block at the domain."
    }
  ]
}

clean is true because the only finding is info: worth knowing, not a problem. explain_rule(code="VOL-001") says why the rule exists and shows a fixed contract.

docs.title: 4. Generate test data
docs.text:
generate_test_data(path="orders.yaml", rows=200, invalid_ratio=0.1, seed=42)

{
  "contract": "orders.yaml",
  "data_file": "test_data/orders.csv",
  "rows": 200,
  "columns": ["order_id", "customer_id", "status", "amount", "_is_invalid", "_test_case_types"],
  "intended_invalid_rows": 20
}

invalid_ratio is a request: 20 of the 200 rows were made to break a rule. The two extra columns mark which rows, and how they were broken; they are test-data markers, not part of your contract.

docs.title: 5. Run it
docs.text:
run_contract(path="orders.yaml", source="test_data/orders.csv", sample=2)

{
  "contract": "orders.yaml",
  "ran": true,
  "engine": "polars",
  "good_rows": 180,
  "quarantined_rows": 20,
  "quarantine_reasons": {
    "Rule failed: status_accepted_values (\"status\" IN ('placed', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'cancelled'))": 10,
    "Rule failed: status_required (\"status\" IS NOT NULL)": 5,
    "Rule failed: customer_id_required (\"customer_id\" IS NOT NULL)": 4,
    "Rule failed: amount_range (\"amount\" >= 0 AND \"amount\" <= 10000)": 4,
    "Rule failed: order_id_required (\"order_id\" IS NOT NULL)": 2,
    "Rule failed: amount_required (\"amount\" IS NOT NULL)": 2
  },
  "quarantined_sample": [
    {
      "order_id": "ORD-658766", "customer_id": null, "status": "placed", "amount": 18.43,
      "_test_case_types": "NOT_NULL_VIOLATION",
      "_lakelogic_errors": ["Rule failed: customer_id_required (\"customer_id\" IS NOT NULL)"]
    },
    {
      "order_id": "ORD-556640", "customer_id": "CUST-526170", "status": "UNKNOWN_VGV", "amount": 28.19,
      "_test_case_types": "ACCEPTED_VALUE_VIOLATION",
      "_lakelogic_errors": ["Rule failed: status_accepted_values (\"status\" IN ('placed', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'cancelled'))"]
    }
  ]
}

(The sample rows are shortened here; the real response carries every column.)

docs.title: Reading the result
docs.text:
• 180 + 20 = 200. Every row is accounted for: none was dropped silently.
  • The 20 quarantined rows are the 20 that were made bad — the rules caught each one.
  • The reasons add up to 27, not 20. A row can break more than one rule (a row with no status fails both status_required and status_accepted_values), and each rule it breaks is counted.
  • quarantined_sample holds up to sample of the quarantined rows, each with the rules it broke. Accepted rows are never returned.
  • required: true is a rule too. The *_required reasons come from the fields, not the quality block.

Nothing was written to the contract's target. To keep the rows, run again with write_outputs=true: they are saved under runs/ in your project.
